title: Asking the way
goal: Ask for and give directions — using the imperative, and choosing between *nach*, *zu* and *in* for the word "to".
bekal: give directions with the imperative (*Gehen Sie…*)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Entschuldigung, wo ist…?
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost in a small town near Potsdam. He stops someone on the sidewalk — and gets a typically German answer: precise, in order, and long.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zum Bahnhof?
lines.id: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?
lines.literal: excuse(-me), how come I to-the station?

lines.speaker: Passantin:
lines.text: Zum Bahnhof? Gehen Sie hier geradeaus bis zur Ampel.
lines.id: To the station? Go straight on from here as far as the traffic lights.
lines.literal: to-the station? go you here straight until to-the traffic-light.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: As far as the traffic lights, OK.

lines.speaker: Passantin:
lines.text: Dann biegen Sie links ab und gehen Sie über die Brücke.
lines.id: Then turn left and go over the bridge.
lines.literal: then turn you left off and go you over the bridge.

lines.speaker: Passantin:
lines.text: Nach der Brücke sehen Sie rechts eine Kirche. Der Bahnhof ist direkt dahinter.
lines.id: After the bridge you'll see a church on the right. The station is right behind it.
lines.literal: after the bridge see you right a church. the station is directly behind-it.

lines.speaker: Passantin:
lines.text: Nein, zehn Minuten zu Fuß. Sie können auch den Bus nehmen, die Linie 6.
lines.id: No, ten minutes on foot. You can also take the bus, number 6.
lines.literal: no, ten minutes to foot. you can also the bus take, the line 6.

lines.speaker: Passantin:
lines.text: Gleich da drüben, vor der Apotheke.
lines.id: Just across the street, in front of the pharmacy.
lines.literal: right there opposite, in-front-of the pharmacy.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vielen Dank! Sie sind sehr nett.
lines.id: Thank you so much! That's very kind of you.
lines.literal: many thanks! you are very kind.

lines.speaker: Passantin:
lines.id: You're welcome. Have a good trip!

notes: ***Wie komme ich zu…?*** is the standard formula for asking the way, and far more useful than *Wo ist…?* because the answer is directions, not just pointing.

**The polite imperative puts *Sie* after the verb.** *Gehen Sie…*, *Biegen Sie…*, *Nehmen Sie…*. Unlike English, the pronoun isn't dropped — and it's precisely its presence that makes the command sound polite.

***abbiegen* is a separable verb**, so the prefix still flies to the end: *Biegen Sie links **ab***. Other separable verbs you'll hear in directions: *einsteigen* (get on), *aussteigen* (get off), *umsteigen* (change, transfer).

**Line 4: *über die Brücke* takes the Akkusativ.** There's movement — you're crossing the bridge — so it isn't *über der Brücke*. Compare line 6: *nach **der** Brücke* (Dativ), because *nach* is always Dativ, no matter what.

***zum* and *zur*.** *zu dem → zum* (masculine & neuter), *zu der → zur* (feminine). *zum Bahnhof*, *zur Ampel*, *zur Apotheke*, *zum Markt*. You'll hear these contractions in almost every set of directions.

***Nichts zu danken*** ("nothing to thank for") is one of several ways to reply to thanks. Others: *Bitte*, *Bitte schön*, *Gern geschehen*, *Kein Problem*. The one you'll hear most is the shortest — *bitte*.

grammars.title: The imperative (Imperativ)
body: There are three forms, one for each way of addressing people. The one you'll use most with strangers is the *Sie* form — and it's the easiest, because it's identical to the normal form, just with the word order flipped.
after: The **du** form is made by dropping *-st* from the normal *du* form: *du gehst → Geh!*, *du kommst → Komm!*, *du machst → Mach!* Verbs whose vowel changes **keep** the new vowel: *du nimmst → Nimm!*, *du sprichst → Sprich!* — but the ones with an Umlaut **lose** it: *du fährst → **Fahr**!*
*Bitte* softens any command, and with strangers it's almost obligatory: *Kommen Sie **bitte** herein!* Without *bitte*, a German imperative really does sound like an order.
To forbid something, just add *nicht*: *Geh **nicht** dorthin!* A softer version uses a modal verb: *Sie dürfen hier nicht parken.*

head: Commands you'll hear
Meaning
rows: Nehmen Sie die zweite Straße links.
Take the second street on the left.
Get off at the main station.

grammars.title: nach, zu or in? Three ways to say "to"
body: English uses one word, "to", for all of these; German divides them by the kind of destination. There are only a few rules, and they don't change.

head: Preposition
Used for
Form
Example
rows: cities, countries without an article, directions
nach Berlin, nach Hause, nach links
people, buildings, places as a destination
zum Arzt, zur Schule, zu meiner Freundin
ins Kino, in die Stadt, in den Supermarkt
going to the edge of something
auf den Markt, auf die Post

after: The difference between *zu* and *in* is subtle but real: *Ich gehe **zur** Schule* means heading for the school (maybe just as far as the gate), while *Ich gehe **in die** Schule* stresses going inside. In everyday speech *zu* is the safest choice.
⚠️ Countries with an article don't take *nach* but *in*: *in **die** Schweiz*, *in **die** Türkei*, *in **die** USA*. There are only a few, and you've seen them all in unit 2.
Fixed phrases to memorize: ***nach Hause*** (home, going home) and ***zu Hause*** (at home). Neither follows any rule, and both are used every day.

blocks.text: Lifesavers if you're truly lost: ***Ich habe mich verlaufen*** ("I'm lost", on foot) or ***Ich suche diese Adresse*** while showing your phone screen. The second one works even if you don't catch a single word of the answer.

Example

blocks.title: Three sentences that get you anywhere
items: *Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zum/zur …?* — Excuse me, how do I get to …?
*Ist das weit von hier?* — Is it far from here?
*Welche Linie fährt zum Bahnhof?* — Which line goes to the station?

blocks.text: ⚠️ In many places you have to **validate** your city transit ticket yourself in a small machine before boarding (*entwerten*). An unvalidated ticket counts as invalid, and the fine is sixty euros — no matter how polite your German is.

items: Entschuldigung, wie komme ich zum Bahnhof?
Gehen Sie geradeaus bis zur Ampel.
Sie können auch den Bus nehmen.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order to make a command.

answers: Excuse me, how do I get to the station? — Go straight on as far as the traffic lights. — Then turn left. — Is it far? — Where's the bus stop? — You can also take the bus.
nach — zum — zur — in — nach — zum
Gehen Sie geradeaus. — Biegen Sie rechts ab. — Nehmen Sie den Bus. — Steigen Sie am Bahnhof aus. — Sprechen Sie bitte langsamer. — Warten Sie bitte einen Moment.
